newsitem.title: FRANCE: French constitution gives Chirac right to set poll.
newsitem.headline: French constitution gives Chirac right to set poll.

text.p: France's 1958 Fifth Republic constitution gives President Jacques Chirac the right to dissolve the National Assembly after consultations with the prime minister and the speakers of both houses of parliament.
A general election must be held 20 to 40 days after a decree is published in the Official Journal dissolving the Assembly.
The president may not dissolve parliament again in the first year of a new legislature.
Bills which have been approved on a first reading remain in limbo and may be reactivated by the newly-elected majority.
The upper house, the Senate, is elected indirectly by local officials and is not affected by dissolution of the Assembly.
A general election is held in two rounds in 577 single-member constituencies. A candidate who wins more than 50 percent of votes cast on the first ballot is elected without a runoff.

Otherwise, any candidate who polls 12.5 percent of the number of registered voters may enter the second ballot. The candidate who wins the most votes on the runoff is elected, even if he or she does not poll 50 percent.

Except for May 30, 1968, when President Charles de Gaulle called a snap election after student-worker protests rocked the country, dissolutions under the Fifth Republic have been carried out by newly-elected presidents seeking a parliamentary majority.
Raymond Barre in 1978 was the last outgoing prime minister to win a general election.
